meta.title: The Product Book: How to Become a Great Product Manager
meta.author: Josh Anon, Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

sentences: In **The Product Book**, authors **Josh Anon** and **Carlos González de Villaumbrosia** introduce readers to the intricacies of **Product Management**.
Whether you're a **newcomer** or an **experienced PM**, this **end-to-end guide** helps understand the PM's role in building products and driving a company's success.
With the **analogy** of PMs being like "**Mini CEOs**," the book explains that PMs must balance **customer needs**, **business strategy**, and **execution**.
It highlights that PMs represent customers, saying '**no**' to unnecessary features while collaborating with **design** and **engineering** to build products efficiently.
**Product School** offers further learning opportunities through flexible courses taught by industry experts.
A **Product Manager (PM)** helps bridge **Design** and **Engineering** teams to solve customer problems.
**Design** includes not just appearance but also **information architecture**, **wireframes**, and **prototypes** for testing.
The final design must be validated with customers and approved by stakeholders.
Once the design is set, PMs oversee building the solution, which varies by company based on product types (e.g., mobile apps vs. hardware).
PMs must prioritize bugs and manage **technical debt**, which can challenge engineers accustomed to writing complete solutions.
Despite outlining this process linearly, real-life development is more **iterative**, with teams revisiting different stages as new use cases arise.

**The second phase, **retention**, is about maintaining user interest after their initial engagement. Companies focus on how often users return to the product. Sustained engagement is more valuable than rapid growth but poor retention because it leads to a stable, growing user base over time. A good product becomes more essential to users as time passes, much like how frequent flyer points incentivize continuous travel on the same airline.**
Social networks are an ideal example, as users invest time in building their audience, discouraging them from switching platforms easily.
On the contrary, products like ride-sharing apps can be easily replaced if competitors offer better incentives, due to lack of user loyalty incentives or significant differences in experience.

parts.title: Opportunities in Metrics and Success Metrics

sentences: **Finding Opportunities in Funnels and Metrics**: Identifying opportunities requires understanding **user behavior** through **funnels and metrics**.
Not every **drop in funnel** is bad; it might filter for the right user behavior.
Combining **segmentation and cohort analysis** can highlight valuable insights, like changes after a big event.
**Improving a metric** is key, aligning with company goals.
**Success vs. Vanity Metrics** by **Beatriz Datangel** stresses focusing on **real user impact metrics** like customer satisfaction and less on high-level, less insightful numbers like **pageviews**.

parts.title: Improving Customer Satisfaction and Validating Ideas

sentences: **Moover.io** aims to **improve customer satisfaction** by reducing friction in its workflow.
The **opportunity hypothesis** suggests that eliminating phone calls with moving companies and consolidating communication into an **in-app messaging tool** will enhance satisfaction for busy users.

To **measure success**, the team will track their **Net Promoter Score (NPS)** and observe the **percentage of customers** who complete the bid-to-move funnel and the **number of messages sent** per customer.
**Validating Hypotheses** involves ensuring the correctness of ideas due to **opportunity costs**.
Product managers need to **distinguish great ideas** from the good ones.
**Building a full product** for an idea is risky and costly, so **lean principles** are employed for **experiment validation**.
This includes using analytics for **internal data validation**, **customer development** for feedback on new products/features, and **experiments like MVPs and A/B tests** to assess workflow changes.
Multiple types of **validation (objective, anecdotal, cost/benefit)** are essential for full opportunity assessment.
**Survey Design** is crucial since you're not present to ask follow-up questions.
Aim to validate your hypothesis by checking how many people have the **pain**, invested in solutions, are dissatisfied, and could use yours.
Keep **surveys** brief due to **survey fatigue**—randomize question order to combat it.
Avoid leading questions, and focus on what customers **have done**, not hypotheticals.
Prioritize **clarity** in language and organize questions from broad to narrow, finishing with a space for additional thoughts.
Ensure queries are about **actual** behavior rather than aspirations.

parts.title: Crafting Clear Project Objectives and Metrics

sentences: As **product managers** (PMs) prepare project requirement documents (PRDs), it's crucial to define clear **objectives** and **success metrics**.
These metrics should highlight what you want the customer to experience and what internal goals to achieve, such as increasing the number of users.
During this process, PMs should recognize metrics that directly impact the success metrics, and not list every **possible metric**.
Effective PMs will note uncertain metrics or goals with "???" and address them in the "**Open Issues**" section.
Clearly defined **messaging** is also essential, although it might need refinement as the project progresses.
Timeline and release planning should be informed by market needs and team capabilities, ensuring the project is ready when needed, such as by a major sales period like a holiday.
Once you decide **what to build** with user research, **information architecture (IA)** designers model how to structure and organize the data.
They decide **what information comes first** and might create a **data model** with diagrams outlining the flow of information, such as an IA diagram for **Moover’s messaging** feature.
**Interaction designers** handle how the product appears and guides user **navigation** through it.
They choose **UI controls** and optimize steps for **common tasks**, often collaborating with engineering on **feasibility**.
Deliverables from this phase include **wireframes**, rough diagrams of user interactions, which can evolve into detailed mock-ups.
**Visual designers** work during or after wireframing, shaping **how the product looks** and aligning it with brand messaging.
They create **mock-ups** showing a pixel-perfect look without functionality.

Prototypers convert wireframes into **interactive prototypes** using tools like **Balsamiq** or **InVision**, which help teams internally understand the product better and aids in estimating technical efforts.
**Prototypes** are also foundational for usability testing, ensuring design solutions meet user needs and remain aligned with **company vision**, like Apple’s design choices.

parts.title: Criticism and Implementation of Agile and Scrum Methods

sentences: **Agile** responds to immediate customer needs, while **Waterfall** focuses on long-term planning.
Both approaches are criticized: Agile for being reactionary, and Waterfall for low success rates in complex projects.
Combining Agile/Lean with an overarching **product vision** can merge short-term flexibility with a planned roadmap.
**Scrum** is a popular Agile method, emphasizing teamwork and self-organized strategy.
PMs have significant input in setting short-term goals but do not micro-manage.
Scrum, often adopted for its structure, involves time-boxed sprints, backlog grooming, and a focus on continuous improvement.
It accommodates change within a project while maintaining a planned trajectory.
Scrum meetings and standards provide a framework to manage larger transitions from **Waterfall to Agile.**
In preparing **products for launch**, it's important to **plan strategically**.
This involves setting clear objectives, identifying targeted phases of testing, and assigning roles to ensure proper execution.
Engineers may need to perform **stress tests** to confirm the system supports the expected demand, as emphasized by past launch failures from companies like **Color**.
The type of **launch event** should align with the product's scope.
Notable examples are **Gmail's successful invite-only beta** versus the **big-bang launch** of Color.
**Small events** or **direct communication** can suffice for less significant features, while **larger events** may suit major product introductions.
Planning requires both identifying the right **audiences** and ensuring **technical readiness**.
